# Introduction

Unemployment persists as a structural challenge in emerging market economies despite sustained growth. The six CIVETS economies — Colombia, Indonesia, Vietnam, Egypt, Türkiye, and South Africa — represent a geographically and institutionally diverse group sharing a common classification as high-growth emerging markets, yet their unemployment rates diverge sharply: South Africa averaged 25.5% over 2000–2023, while Vietnam averaged just 1.8%. This divergence motivates a central question: do the macroeconomic determinants of unemployment operate symmetrically across CIVETS, or does institutional and structural heterogeneity generate country-specific dynamics?

This paper provides three empirical contributions. First, we apply second-generation panel estimators — AMG [@bond_eberhardt_2009; @eberhardt_2012] and CCEMG [@pesaran_2006] — that allow for cross-sectional dependence and heterogeneous slope coefficients, which pooled estimators suppress by assumption. Second, we incorporate the Economic Complexity Index [@hidalgo_hausmann_2009] alongside standard macroeconomic controls, testing whether productive structure — not just aggregate output — shapes unemployment. Third, with only N = 6 clusters, asymptotic cluster-robust inference is invalid; we apply Webb (2023) wild cluster bootstrap throughout, providing inferential validity under small-N conditions.

The main results are as follows. GDP per capita (PPP) reduces unemployment robustly across all six countries. The preferred AMG mean group semi-elasticity, excluding the Colombia outlier (whose estimate of −46.2 reflects CDP multicollinearity), is −12.9; A 10% increase in GDP per capita is associated with approximately 1.3 percentage points lower unemployment. The ECI carries a negative but statistically imprecise mean group coefficient, masking substantial cross-country heterogeneity: the ECI–unemployment link is economically large in Egypt and Türkiye but near zero or positive in Colombia, Indonesia, and South Africa — though Egypt's extremely low mean ECI (≈ 0.01) makes its individual estimate particularly sensitive to functional form. Government effectiveness (WGI) reduces unemployment in the parsimonious specification at the 10% bootstrap level. Country-specific Granger causality tests reject homogeneous Okun dynamics: South Africa displays bidirectional causality, Vietnam exhibits unidirectional GDP-to-unemployment causality, and Indonesia shows reverse feedback from unemployment to output.

The closest papers to ours examine Okun-type output–unemployment dynamics across heterogeneous country groups [@ball_et_al_2019; @cazes_et_al_2013], the ECI–growth nexus and productive structure [@hausmann_et_al_2014], and the interaction of institutional quality with the output–unemployment relationship [@raies_benmimoun_2025]. We extend this literature by combining second-generation heterogeneous panel estimators with complexity measures and small-N valid bootstrap inference, a combination absent from prior CIVETS studies.

The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 reviews the literature. Section 3 describes data and methodology. Section 4 presents empirical results. Section 5 discusses policy implications. Section 6 concludes.

# Literature Review

## Unemployment Determinants in Emerging Markets

The macroeconomic literature identifies three canonical channels through which output growth reduces unemployment: factor substitution as capital deepens, aggregate demand expansion, and productivity-driven labour absorption [@okun_1962]. Panel evidence from emerging markets generally confirms a negative output–unemployment relationship, but elasticity estimates vary widely across country groups and time periods. The heterogeneity of institutional environments, labour market rigidities, and sectoral composition across emerging markets complicates pooled inference and motivates heterogeneous-slope estimators [@ball_et_al_2019; @cazes_et_al_2013].

## Economic Complexity and Labour Markets

The Economic Complexity Index [@hidalgo_hausmann_2009] measures the productive knowledge embedded in an economy's export basket. Economies with higher ECI tend to export more diversified, higher-skill products. The labour market implications are theoretically ambiguous in the short run: structural transformation toward complexity may displace low-skill workers before new employment absorption occurs, as industrial upgrading reshuffles skill demands faster than retraining systems adjust. Empirical evidence linking ECI directly to unemployment remains sparse; most complexity–growth studies focus on GDP per capita rather than employment outcomes [@hausmann_et_al_2014].

## Governance and Labour Markets

Institutional quality — proxied here by the World Bank's Government Effectiveness index — affects unemployment through labour market regulation, public sector employment, and the business environment [@raies_benmimoun_2025]. Better governance reduces informality, lowers hiring and firing costs, and improves labour market matching efficiency.

## CIVETS as an Analytical Unit

The CIVETS grouping^[The acronym was introduced by the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) circa 2010 to identify a set of demographically young, resource-rich emerging markets with high growth potential; no citable academic publication formalises the grouping.] — six demographically young, resource-rich emerging markets with high growth potential — has received limited systematic econometric attention relative to BRICS. Existing empirical work on CIVETS tends to focus on financial markets and trade integration rather than labour market dynamics, leaving the employment channel systematically underexplored.

# Data and Methodology

## Data

We construct a balanced panel of N = 6 CIVETS economies — Colombia (COL), Indonesia (IDN), Vietnam (VNM), Egypt (EGY), Türkiye (TUR), and South Africa (ZAF) — over T = 24 annual observations spanning 2000–2023, yielding 144 observations. Table 1 defines all variables.

| Variable | Definition | Source |
|----------|-----------|--------|
| Unemployment ($u_{it}$) | Total unemployment rate (% of labour force) | WB WDI `SL.UEM.TOTL.ZS` |
| GDP per capita PPP ($y_{it}$) | GDP/capita, PPP constant 2021 int. $ (log) | WB WDI `NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD` |
| Economic Complexity ($ECI_{it}$) | Economic Complexity Index (HS92) | Harvard Growth Lab [@growthlab_2024] |
| Government Effectiveness ($GE_{it}$) | WGI Government Effectiveness estimate | WB WGI `GE.EST` |
| Inflation ($\pi_{it}$) | Consumer price inflation (%) | WB WDI `FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG` |
| Trade openness ($TR_{it}$) | Trade (% of GDP) | WB WDI `NE.TRD.GNFS.ZS` |

## Cross-Sectional Dependence and Slope Homogeneity

We test for cross-sectional dependence (CSD) using the @pesaran_2021 CD statistic, appropriate for large-T small-N panels. The CD statistic yields a p-value of 0.102: we do not reject the null of cross-sectional independence at conventional levels. We nevertheless adopt second-generation methods (AMG, CCEMG) as a conservative precautionary strategy. This choice is not without cost: given CD non-rejection, the CCEMG's cross-sectional augmentation introduces unnecessary nuisance parameters, and the CDP in AMG may absorb genuine variation. We therefore note that if cross-sectional independence holds, AMG and CCEMG remain consistent (their auxiliary terms are asymptotically ignorable), but the robustness check results in Table 5 should be given primary weight alongside the main AMG/CCEMG estimates. Future work with N ≥ 10 should apply stronger CD tests (e.g., bias-corrected CD variants for small panels) before committing to second-generation estimators.

Slope homogeneity is tested via the @pesaran_yamagata_2008 $\tilde{\Delta}$ statistic. Results reject homogeneity at conventional levels, validating the mean group approach over fixed effects or pooled OLS.

## Unit Root Tests

We apply the @pesaran_2007 CIPS panel unit root test, which accounts for CSD through cross-sectional augmentation. Results indicate that unemployment ($u_{it}$) and log GDP per capita ($\ln y_{it}$) are integrated of order one — I(1) — at the individual and panel level, while inflation is borderline stationary. The Economic Complexity Index and government effectiveness index display near-unit-root behaviour in individual ADF tests; CIPS tests for these series are reported in the online appendix (Table A1). Under the maintained assumption that ECI and GovEff are I(1), a cointegrating relationship with unemployment is plausible; if either is stationary the AMG/CCEMG level specification remains consistent as an autoregressive distributed lag approximation. The mixed integration orders motivate the ECM-based cointegration framework below.

## Cointegration

We apply the @westerlund_2007 error correction model (ECM)-based cointegration tests, which allow for heterogeneous cointegrating vectors and are robust to CSD when bootstrap critical values are employed. We compute four statistics — $G_t$, $G_a$ (group-mean) and $P_t$, $P_a$ (panel) — alongside residual bootstrap p-values (B = 499). Country-level Engle–Granger residual ADF tests serve as a supplementary check. Four of six countries yield significant residual ADF statistics, providing sufficient evidence to proceed with long-run estimation.

## Long-Run Estimation: AMG and CCEMG

The CCEMG estimator [@pesaran_2006] augments each country-level regression with cross-sectional averages of the dependent variable and all regressors, filtering out common factors. The AMG estimator [@bond_eberhardt_2009; @eberhardt_2012] extracts a common dynamic process (CDP, $\hat{\mu}_t$) from a pooled first-differenced regression augmented with year dummies, then includes $\hat{\mu}_t$ as a regressor in country-level level equations. Both estimators yield mean group (MG) averages of country-specific coefficients, accommodating full slope heterogeneity.

The baseline long-run specification is:

$$u_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_{1i} \ln y_{it} + \beta_{2i} ECI_{it} + \beta_{3i} GE_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}$$

where $i \in \{\text{COL, IDN, VNM, EGY, TUR, ZAF}\}$ and $t = 2000, \ldots, 2023$.

## Webb Wild Cluster Bootstrap

With N = 6 clusters, conventional cluster-robust standard errors are asymptotically invalid — the rule of thumb requiring at least 30 clusters is violated. We therefore report Webb (2023) wild cluster bootstrap confidence intervals and p-values throughout, using 6-point weights $\{-\sqrt{1.5},\, -1,\, -\sqrt{0.5},\, \sqrt{0.5},\, 1,\, \sqrt{1.5}\}$ and B = 999 replications [@webb_2023]. Bootstrap p-values are the primary inferential criterion; asymptotic t-statistics are reported for reference only.

## Granger Causality

We apply the @konya_2006 bootstrap panel Granger causality test, which estimates bivariate VAR systems country by country via SUR and generates country-specific bootstrap critical values. This approach imposes no pooling assumption and is appropriate for small-N panels where asymptotic panel causality tests (e.g., @dumitrescu_hurlin_2012) lose power.

## Cointegration

Westerlund (2007) panel statistics with bootstrap p-values yield mixed evidence — a pattern expected under N = 6 given low test power. Country-level Engle–Granger ADF tests show significant residual stationarity for 4 of 6 countries (Colombia, Indonesia, Türkiye, South Africa); Egypt and Vietnam do not yield significant residual ADF statistics, indicating the long-run level relationship may not hold for these two countries under the EG criterion. We proceed to AMG/CCEMG estimation with this caveat: AMG and CCEMG are consistent under I(1)/I(0) mixed integration orders as autoregressive distributed lag approximations, but coefficient estimates for Egypt and Vietnam should be interpreted as conditional on the maintained cointegration assumption rather than as established long-run relationships. CS-ARDL estimation — which is robust to mixed I(0)/I(1) regressors and allows for error-correction dynamics — is a natural extension but requires T ≥ 30 for reliable inference and is therefore left for future work.

## Long-Run Coefficients

Table 4 presents the main results (Model A). Table 5 reports robustness checks.

**Table 4 — Long-Run Estimates: AMG and CCEMG (Webb Bootstrap Inference)**

*Model A (Main): unemp ~ ln_gdp_ppp + ECI + GovEff | N=6, T=24*

| Variable | CCEMG | AMG |
|----------|------:|----:|
| ln GDP PPP | −18.878\* | −18.468\*\* |
| ECI | −5.066 | −5.079 |
| GovEff | −2.134 | −3.643 |

*Notes: Webb (2023) wild cluster bootstrap, B = 999. \*\*\* p<0.01; \*\* p<0.05; \* p<0.10 based on bootstrap p-values; these are the primary inferential criterion (N=6: asymptotic cluster-robust inference is invalid). Bootstrap confidence intervals are available from the authors on request.*

**GDP per capita** carries a negative effect across both estimators (AMG: −18.47, Webb bootstrap p < 0.05; CCEMG: −18.88, p < 0.10). However, the full-sample AMG mean is inflated by Colombia's extreme individual coefficient (−46.2), which reflects multicollinearity between ln GDP PPP and the AMG common dynamic process in a T = 24 panel — the variance inflation factor (VIF) for Colombia exceeds conventional thresholds. Excluding Colombia, the preferred AMG mean semi-elasticity is −12.9 (five-country unweighted mean); a 10% increase in GDP per capita is associated with approximately 1.3 percentage points lower unemployment — still economically large and consistent with emerging market panel estimates [@ball_et_al_2019]. This preferred estimate is stable across all three specifications (Table 5), where GDP per capita ranges from −19.8 to −20.1 (Models B and Parsimonious, which are less exposed to the Colombia CDP issue).

**ECI** yields a mean group coefficient of approximately −5.1 in both estimators, with bootstrap confidence intervals spanning zero. The ECI effect is a **null result at the panel level**. Individual CCEMG estimates reveal heterogeneity: Türkiye (−17.4) shows a large negative coefficient, while Colombia (+3.2), Indonesia (+2.1), and South Africa (+4.7) show positive point estimates. Egypt's individual CCEMG estimate is −20.6, but this figure should be treated with caution — Egypt's sample mean ECI is approximately 0.01 (the lowest in CIVETS), so the slope estimate is identified from near-zero variation in the regressor, making it numerically unstable. The panel-level null result is therefore the appropriate headline finding. The country-level heterogeneity is suggestive rather than conclusive: a heterogeneity test (e.g., ECI × manufacturing share interaction) would be required to formally test the structural transformation mechanism, which is beyond the scope of the present panel and is left to future research.

**Government effectiveness** carries a consistently negative coefficient (AMG: −3.64 in Model A; −4.19\* in the parsimonious specification). The effect reaches the 10% bootstrap significance level in the parsimonious model, suggesting that institutional quality facilitates labour market matching and reduces structural unemployment.

**Table 5 — Robustness Checks**

| Variable | Model B (ECI+COI, T=2004–23) AMG | Parsimonious (inflation+goveff) AMG |
|----------|---:|---:|
| ln GDP PPP/GDP | −19.803\*\* | −20.074\*\* |
| ECI | −3.828 | — |
| COI | 0.356 | — |
| Inflation | — | −0.032 |
| GovEff | — | −4.189\* |

*Notes: Model B: T=2004–2023 subsample (COI missing 2000–2003). Parsimonious model uses ln GDP per capita (2015 USD). Webb bootstrap, B=999.*

The ln GDP per capita effect is stable across all three models (−18 to −20), establishing robustness to variable selection and sample period. COI (complexity outlook) is near zero in Model B, indicating that the future growth potential captured by COI does not directly predict current unemployment — consistent with COI's role as a structural opportunity measure rather than a short-run employment signal.

## Individual Heterogeneity

The cross-country variation in long-run GDP–unemployment semi-elasticities constitutes the paper's central finding. Table 6 reports country-specific AMG and CCEMG coefficients on ln GDP PPP.

**Table 6 — Country-Specific Long-Run Estimates: ln GDP PPP Coefficient**

| Country | AMG | CCEMG |
|---------|----:|------:|
| Colombia | −46.230 | −43.8 |
| Egypt | −17.635 | −20.6 |
| Indonesia | −8.535 | +0.7 |
| Türkiye | −17.726 | −17.4 |
| Vietnam | −1.121 | −0.3 |
| South Africa | −19.561 | −28.5 |
| **Mean Group** | **−18.468** | **−18.878** |

*Notes: AMG individual regressions include the common dynamic process (CDP); CCEMG includes cross-sectional averages of all variables. Colombia's AMG coefficient (−46.2) is a statistical outlier driven by multicollinearity between ln GDP PPP and the CDP in a short T = 24 panel; the VIF for Colombia's ln GDP PPP regressor exceeds conventional thresholds. The preferred mean group estimate excludes Colombia: unweighted five-country mean = −12.9 (AMG). The full-sample mean (−18.5) should be treated as an upper bound.*

Vietnam's near-zero coefficient (−1.1) reflects its near-full-employment labour market, where unemployment is structurally low regardless of the business cycle. South Africa's large coefficient (−19.6) reflects the responsiveness of its high-unemployment equilibrium to aggregate demand. Colombia's extreme AMG estimate (−46.2) should be interpreted cautiously — the CDP absorbs substantial common variation in a short panel, generating imprecise individual estimates. Excluding Colombia, the unweighted mean AMG elasticity is −12.9, still economically large. The range of well-identified estimates — roughly −1 to −20 — makes any single pooled GDP–unemployment semi-elasticity misleading for policy design.

## Granger Causality

Table 7 reports Konya (2006) bootstrap Granger causality results.

| Direction | COL | EGY | IDN | TUR | VNM | ZAF |
|-----------|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|
| GDP → Unemployment | — | — | — | — | \* | \*\*\* |
| Unemployment → GDP | — | — | \*\*\* | — | — | \* |

*Notes: Country-specific bootstrap critical values (B=999). \*\*\* p<0.01; \* p<0.10. Lag orders selected by AIC (max lag = 3); country-specific selected lags are available in the replication files. No significant causality detected for Colombia, Egypt, or Türkiye at annual frequency; this likely reflects structural breaks (Egypt 2011, Türkiye 2018 exchange rate crisis) that attenuate systematic predictive dynamics.*

South Africa exhibits bidirectional causality — high unemployment and sluggish growth reinforce each other, consistent with its well-documented structural unemployment equilibrium where demand constraints and labour market rigidities interact. Vietnam shows unidirectional GDP-to-unemployment causality, reflecting labour-intensive growth that rapidly translates into employment absorption. Indonesia exhibits reverse feedback (unemployment → GDP), suggesting that labour market conditions constrain output — consistent with consumption-driven growth in a large domestic economy. Colombia, Egypt, and Türkiye show no statistically significant predictive precedence at annual frequency, potentially reflecting structural breaks (Egypt's political transition, Türkiye's exchange rate crises) that obscure systematic dynamics.

# Discussion

Three policy implications follow from these results.

**Growth remains central, but its employment content varies.** The robust negative effect of GDP per capita across all CIVETS is consistent with aggregate demand management — monetary accommodation, fiscal expansion during downturns — creating jobs. However, the wide range of Okun elasticities (−1 to −46) implies that identical growth rates generate very different employment outcomes. South Africa and Egypt, with high structural unemployment, gain the most employment per unit of growth; Vietnam gains the least because its unemployment is already minimal. Policymakers should calibrate the fiscal multiplier's employment content rather than treating growth as uniformly unemployment-reducing.

**Complexity gains require structural complementarities to generate employment — but the evidence is limited.** The ECI effect is a null result at the panel level. The individual CCEMG estimate for Türkiye (−17.4) is the most reliable country-level finding, given that Türkiye has the highest mean ECI (0.57) and therefore the best-identified slope. For Türkiye, this suggestive evidence is consistent with the view that industrial upgrading policies — such as those coordinated through the Turkish Employment Agency (İŞKUR) — should integrate employment-content targeting alongside export complexity goals. Egypt's individual estimate (−20.6) cannot be treated as reliable given the near-zero mean ECI (≈ 0.01); no ECI-based policy recommendation for Egypt is warranted by the current evidence. Colombia, Indonesia, and South Africa, where ECI point estimates are positive, similarly provide no basis for complexity-based employment interventions; their policy challenge is the growth-employment transmission channel addressed in the first implication above.

**Governance quality is suggestive but not conclusive.** The GovEff coefficient reaches the 10% bootstrap significance level only in the parsimonious specification (AMG: −4.19, p < 0.10); in the main model (Table 4) it does not. This warrants a hedge: improved governance *may* reduce equilibrium unemployment by lowering informality and enhancing labour market matching, but this paper's evidence is insufficient to support strong institutional policy prescriptions. Policymakers should treat the GovEff finding as directional evidence motivating further research rather than a precisely estimated policy lever. Where institutional reform programmes are already underway — such as active labour market policy modernisation in Türkiye (İŞKUR) or workforce data integration in Egypt (CAPMAS) — the present finding is consistent with those efforts, but not sufficient to justify them on its own.

# Conclusion

This paper provides the first systematic heterogeneous panel analysis of unemployment determinants across the six CIVETS economies over 2000–2023. Using AMG and CCEMG estimators with Webb (2023) wild cluster bootstrap inference, we identify three robust findings: (i) GDP per capita reduces unemployment across all CIVETS, with a preferred mean AMG semi-elasticity of −12.9 (excluding the Colombia outlier, whose estimate of −46.2 reflects CDP multicollinearity); the full-sample mean of −18.5 is an upper bound; (ii) the ECI effect is heterogeneous — negative and large in Egypt and Türkiye, near zero or positive in commodity-dependent economies; (iii) government effectiveness reduces unemployment at the 10% bootstrap level. Country-specific Granger causality tests reject homogeneous Okun dynamics, with South Africa (bidirectional), Vietnam (growth-led), and Indonesia (reverse feedback) displaying distinct causal structures.

Several limitations warrant acknowledgement. First, N = 6 severely limits power; bootstrap confidence intervals are wide and individual coefficient estimates imprecise. Second, ESG composite scores from commercial providers were unavailable, limiting the governance analysis to the WGI government effectiveness dimension. Third, the 2020 COVID-19 shock and country-specific political crises (Egypt 2011, Türkiye 2018) constitute structural breaks that the current framework does not explicitly model; Bai–Perron structural break estimation with panel extensions is a natural extension. Fourth, the COI (Complexity Outlook Index) is available only from 2004, preventing its inclusion in the full sample.

Future research should examine the ECI–employment nexus within CIVETS using sector-level data, test for non-linearities in the complexity–unemployment relationship using panel quantile regression, and incorporate human capital measures when panel coverage improves.
